extracted.intended_audience: comics creators, students of comics studies, scholars of visual narrative, and general readers interested in comics theory
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative criteria for understanding, analysing, and creating comics—covering definition, visual grammar, character design, narrative sequencing, and stylistic choices as presented in Scott McCloud's Understanding Comics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of comics — primacy of sequences of images
rubrics_metrics.description: The book's overarching argument is that comics are defined by the primacy of sequences of images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comics should be evaluated/constructed first as sequences; meaning and story emerge from the arrangement and relationship of images over time. This is the foundational criterion McCloud uses to distinguish comics from other media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure — reader's role in completing narrative between panels
rubrics_metrics.description: "Closure" — refers to a reader's role in closing narrative gaps between comics panels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comics rely on readers to infer action, time, emotion, and cause-and-effect across panel transitions. Effective sequential storytelling deliberately creates actionable gaps that engage the reader's imagination; failure to support closure (confusing transitions, missing beats) weakens comprehension and narrative flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonlinear narratives through reader choices and interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Comics employ nonlinear narratives because they rely on the reader's choices and interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because pacing and path through panels can be influenced by layout and reader attention, creators can design nonlinearity (branching, ambiguous sequencing, variable pacing). Evaluate whether a comic's layout and design intentionally invite or hinder reader-driven narrative ordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual literacy — ability to read visual narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: The book begins with discussion of the concept of visual literacy and a history of narrative in visual media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of comics should consider the intended audience's visual literacy: how well the work uses visual conventions, symbols, and sequencing to convey meaning. Educational and critical appreciation depends on clear use of visual grammar and awareness of historical visual techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masking — use of simplistic/archetypal characters to foster identification
rubrics_metrics.description: "Masking": a visual style, dramatic convention, and literary technique — the use of simplistic, archetypal, narrative characters even if juxtaposed with detailed, photographic, verisimilar backgrounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Masking functions as a "mask" for projective identification: a familiar, minimally detailed character allows stronger emotional connection and easier viewer identification. Creators can intentionally use masking to invite reader empathy; critics should note when over-detailing or under-defining a character reduces identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iconic versus realistic representation — stylistic tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: McCloud highlights differences between iconic and realistic figures: iconic figures resemble standard cartoons, while realistic figures focus on photo-quality detail; Western culture is more captivated by iconic images due to their simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating art style, consider how iconic or realistic depiction affects reader engagement, narrative tone, and identification. Iconic styles often increase universality and emotional projection; realism can provide specificity and spectacle. The choice should align with narrative goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Big Triangle — tool for locating and comparing art styles
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Big Triangle": realistic representation in one corner, iconic/cartoon-style in another, and abstraction at the apex; allows placement and grouping of artists by triangulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Big Triangle as an analytic rubric to position an artist's stylistic choices and to compare approaches across works. It helps critique consistency, intended audience, and how style supports or conflicts with narrative content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependent combination of words and pictures (cartooning and panel borders)
rubrics_metrics.description: McCloud cites Töpffer's use of "cartooning and panel borders" as the first interdependent combination of words and pictures seen in Europe; comics depend on the interdependence of words and images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether text and image are integrated (each enhancing the other) or merely co-present. Good comics make words and pictures interdependent—neither redundant nor disconnected. Pay attention to how lettering, captions, and word-balloon placement interact with image sequencing and panel design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequencing and panel grammar — the formal vocabulary of comics
rubrics_metrics.description: The book explores formal aspects of comics: vocabulary and methods of the medium, emphasizing sequences, panel borders, and choices in composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess comics by their use of panel rhythm, gutters, framing, and composition to control time and emphasis. Effective use of panel grammar guides reader pacing and meaning; poor use (jarring rhythms, unclear gutters) impedes comprehension. Consider how layout choices shape narrative timing and focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical antecedents and formal context as evaluative frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding Comics situates comics in a history of visual narrative (e.g., Bayeux Tapestry, Rodolphe Töpffer as 'father of the modern comic') and treats historical forms as antecedents to modern comics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical evaluation and creation benefit from awareness of historical precedents and how contemporary choices echo or diverge from them. Use history to justify formal choices or to innovate deliberately; note when a work ignores relevant conventions or traditions without reason.
